title: JD Vance Casts Doubt on Livestreamed Execution, Says He Will Not Watch It
excerpt: The Pentagon plans a December 3 firing-squad execution for the Fort Hood shooter with the public invited to watch — but the vice president doubts the broadcast will happen and Trump stopped short of endorsing it.
body:
• Vice President JD Vance said Friday he will not watch the Pentagon's planned livestream of the Fort Hood shooter's firing-squad execution — and cast doubt it will even happen: "I don't know that that's actually going to happen."
  • Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced Thursday that former Army psychiatrist Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009, will be executed by firing squad on December 3, with the public able to watch.
  • It would be the first US military firing-squad execution since 1945 and the first public execution in America since 1936 — drawing condemnation from Catholic bishops, some Republican lawmakers, and death-penalty opponents.
  • President Trump backed the execution Friday, saying Hasan "deserves it," but stopped short of clearly endorsing the broadcast, leaving the final decision to the Pentagon.

A Vice President Who Won't Watch

Vice President JD Vance distanced himself Friday from the Pentagon's most provocative announcement in years: a livestreamed firing-squad execution. Speaking to reporters while campaigning in Ohio, Vance — a convert to Catholicism — said he was unconvinced the broadcast would actually materialize despite Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's Thursday announcement. "I've seen his announcements. I don't know that that's actually going to happen," Vance said. "If it's ultimately livestreamed, I'm not gonna be watching it."

https://youtube.com/watch?v=pqQUGpAjKjQ

Hegseth had told the conservative outlet Real America's Voice on Wednesday that Nidal Malik Hasan's execution by "a firing squad of soldiers" on December 3 would be made available for the public to see. "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public," Hegseth said. "Because people need to understand that there are serious consequences for these types of things." Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, opened fire inside a medical building at Fort Hood, Texas, on November 5, 2009, killing 13 people and wounding 32. He was convicted of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder, and sentenced to death in 2013.

Trump Backs the Execution — the Broadcast, Less Clear

President Donald Trump weighed in Friday as he departed the White House, endorsing the firing squad for a man he called a "maniac." "We're giving a man the death penalty who killed 14 soldiers a couple of years ago," Trump said. "Death penalty through firing squad — and, uh, and he deserves it." Trump said he had signed off on the plan — "Absolutely, I approved" — but did not make clear whether his approval extended to Hegseth's livestreaming proposal, and suggested the Pentagon was still making a final determination on a broadcast.

Vance tried to redirect the debate back to the crime. "Whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don't forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people," he said, calling the 2009 shooting "the worst terrorist attack on American soil outside of 9/11."

The Backlash

The announcement triggered condemnation across the political spectrum. Republican Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina called the livestream idea "beyond disgusting" in a social media post. "Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do," Tillis wrote. "It should not be happening in America."

"It is with shock and great sorrow that I have learned of the Department of War's decision to publicly livestream the execution. Our God is the God of life. In no way can Hassan's actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death."

— Archbishop Paul S. Coakley, president, US Conference of Catholic Bishops

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr told CNBC he didn't expect a broadcasting-regulatory role, since the execution is "not on broadcast TV." The last documented public execution in the United States was in 1936, when about 20,000 people attended the hanging of Rainey Bethea in Owensboro, Kentucky. The last US military firing-squad execution was on January 31, 1945, when Pvt. Eddie Slovik was executed for desertion.

What Comes Next

The execution is scheduled for December 3 at Fort Hood, the same Texas base where Hasan carried out the shooting. Between now and then, the Pentagon will have to decide whether Hegseth's promise of a public broadcast survives the legal, logistical, and political headwinds — including from the administration's own vice president, who has now said twice that he won't be watching. Whatever the method, Hasan's case has already forced an uncomfortable national question: whether a public execution is a deterrent America wants to stage, or a spectacle it should refuse to become.
